requirements: The paper "Transverse-Dominant Anisotropic Dispersion and Transient Trapping in 3D Solenoidal Turbulence" has been reproduced.

sub_tasks.requirements: The required turbulence dataset, derived fields, and large-scale filtered fields are available
The public DNS velocity-field dataset for subsonic, isothermal turbulence in a periodic cubic domain has been acquired or otherwise made available
The dataset represents a periodic cubic domain with side length L = 1
The dataset represents purely solenoidal/divergence-free forcing at the largest scales
The forcing modes retained for the large-scale analysis correspond to wavenumbers n = 1-3
A sequence of 200 evenly spaced velocity-field snapshots can be loaded for analysis
The code records or infers the physical time associated with each velocity-field snapshot
Auxiliary Eulerian fields are computed from the instantaneous velocity field
The velocity gradient tensor ∇v is computed on the grid with a documented finite-difference or spectral differentiation convention
The vorticity field is computed as ω = ∇ × v
The antisymmetric rotation tensor is computed as Ω = 1/2(∇v - (∇v)^T)
The symmetric strain-rate tensor is computed as S = 1/2(∇v + (∇v)^T)
The Q-criterion field is computed as Q = 1/2(||Ω||^2 - ||S||^2)
Grid cells with Q > 0 are identified as vortex-core regions where rotation dominates strain
The large-scale velocity field used for anisotropy analysis is computed
A Fourier-space representation of each velocity-field snapshot is computed
A sharp spectral filter retaining only the driving modes n = 1-3 is applied
The filtered field V_LS(x,t) is transformed back to physical space for interpolation along tracer paths
The filtering implementation preserves the vector components of the velocity field and does not replace V_LS with the full unfiltered velocity field
Passive Lagrangian tracer integration is implemented as described in Section 2.2
The tracer ensemble is initialized correctly
8,000 passive Lagrangian tracers are initialized
Tracer initial positions are randomly seeded within the periodic domain
The random seed or initialization procedure is recorded so that the experiment can be rerun
Tracer trajectories are integrated according to dx/dt = v(x(t), t)
A fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) time integration scheme is implemented for tracer advection
The velocity v(x,t) at arbitrary tracer positions is obtained by trilinear interpolation from surrounding grid points
Time interpolation or snapshot-to-snapshot stepping is handled consistently with the spacing of the velocity snapshots
10 integration sub-steps are taken between consecutive velocity-field snapshots
Periodic boundary conditions are enforced at every integration sub-step using a modulo operation on tracer coordinates
The code separately tracks wrapped positions for interpolation and unwrapped displacements for MSD calculations, or otherwise documents and validates the displacement convention used
The local large-scale velocity and Q-criterion are sampled along tracer paths
The same interpolation and integration-time convention used for v(x,t) is used to obtain V_LS(x(t),t) along each tracer trajectory
The Q-criterion value Q(x(t),t) is interpolated along each tracer trajectory
The trajectory output contains positions, displacements, local V_LS values, Q values, and boundary-crossing information required by downstream analyses
The MSD, scaling-exponent, diffusion, and conditional-trapping analyses are implemented
The ensemble Mean-Square Displacement analysis is implemented
For each lag time t, tracer displacements are computed as Δx(t) = x(t0 + t) - x(t0)
MSD(t) is computed as the ensemble average <|Δx(t)|^2> over tracers and valid time origins
The implementation documents whether single-origin or multi-origin lag averaging is used
MSD results are stored as a time series over lag time
The local logarithmic MSD scaling exponent α(t) is implemented
α(t) is computed as d(log MSD)/d(log t) using a numerically stable derivative or local regression method
The implementation handles early-time and late-time derivative boundary effects explicitly
The ballistic, superdiffusive, diffusive, and saturation regimes are identified from α(t)
The classical diffusion coefficient is estimated from the velocity autocorrelation function
The velocity autocorrelation function VACF(t) = <v(t0) · v(t0 + t)> is computed from tracer or field-sampled velocities
The diffusion coefficient D is estimated by integrating the VACF before the onset of finite-domain saturation
The estimated diffusion coefficient is reported and compared with the target D ≈ 0.010
Finite-domain saturation and boundary crossings are measured
The theoretical saturation scale L^2/6 is computed for L = 1 and reported as approximately 0.167
The fraction of tracers that cross at least one periodic boundary by the end of the simulation is computed
The boundary-crossing fraction is compared with the target value of approximately 82.9%
Late-time α(t) < 1 is interpreted as geometric saturation rather than physical subdiffusion
The conditional MSD analysis for trapped and free cohorts is implemented
For each tracer, a vortex-residence fraction or equivalent Q>0 occupancy measure is computed
The Trapped cohort is defined using the top 20% of Q-criterion residence
A Free cohort of least-trapped tracers is defined consistently and documented
Separate MSD curves are computed for the Trapped and Free cohorts
The results show that the Trapped cohort has systematically lower MSD than the Free cohort over the reported lag range
The transverse-dominant anisotropic dispersion analysis is implemented
Parallel and perpendicular displacement components are computed relative to the instantaneous local large-scale velocity
For each tracer and lag, the unit vector V_hat_LS is computed from V_LS(x(t0 + t), t0 + t)
Cases where |V_LS| is zero or numerically tiny are handled explicitly and documented
The parallel MSD is computed as MSD_parallel(t) = <(Δx(t) · V_hat_LS)^2>
The perpendicular displacement is computed as Δx(t) - (Δx(t) · V_hat_LS)V_hat_LS
The perpendicular MSD is computed as MSD_perpendicular(t) = <|Δx(t) - (Δx(t) · V_hat_LS)V_hat_LS|^2>
The implementation clearly preserves the paper's convention that the perpendicular term is the squared magnitude of the full two-dimensional transverse component
The dynamic anisotropy ratio λ(t) is computed and analyzed
λ(t) is computed as MSD_parallel(t) / MSD_perpendicular(t)
The early-time ballistic phase where λ > 1 is identified
The peak anisotropy ratio is reported and compared with the target λ ≈ 2.96 for t < 0.5
The post-ballistic reversal where λ drops below unity after approximately t = 0.5 is identified
The post-ballistic mean anisotropy ratio is computed for t > 0.5
The post-ballistic mean is compared with the target λ ≈ 0.52 ± 0.045
The interpretation of anisotropy is supported by the implemented outputs
The code reports that λ < 1 corresponds to perpendicular dispersion exceeding parallel dispersion under the paper's definition
The analysis connects the transverse-dominant result to the solenoidal large-scale velocity field rather than to an unrelated coordinate axis
The vortex trapping and Q-autocorrelation analysis is implemented
Vortex residence signals are computed along tracer paths
A tracer is classified as inside a vortex core at time t if Q(x(t),t) > 0
For each tracer, the binary Q>0 residence signal is recorded over time
For each tracer, the raw Q(x(t),t) signal is recorded over time for autocorrelation analysis
Vortex residence fractions are computed for each tracer from the Q>0 signal
The Lagrangian autocorrelation function of the Q-criterion signal is implemented
The autocorrelation is computed along tracer trajectories rather than from a fixed Eulerian Q field alone
The autocorrelation function is normalized by its initial value so that the 1/e crossing is meaningful
The characteristic residence time τ_Q is defined as the first time where the normalized autocorrelation decays to 1/e
Interpolation or a documented discrete crossing rule is used to estimate the 1/e crossing time
The τ_Q result is reported and compared with the target τ_Q ≈ 0.200
The large-eddy turnover-time comparison is implemented
The rms velocity v_rms is computed or set consistently with the paper's value v_rms ≈ 0.38
The large-eddy turnover time is computed as T_e = L / v_rms
The reported turnover time is compared with the target T_e ≈ 1 / 0.38 ≈ 2.6
The normalized residence time τ_Q / T_e is computed
The normalized residence time is compared with the target τ_Q / T_e ≈ 0.077, or about 7-8% of a large-eddy turnover time
The conclusion that vortex trapping is transient is tested
The result analysis states whether Q-autocorrelation decays rapidly enough to rule out long-lived trapping under the paper's criterion
The analysis distinguishes transient vortex trapping from sustained anomalous transport or long-term memory
The displacement-PDF, Gaussianity, kurtosis, and Lévy-tail analyses are implemented
Single-component tracer displacement PDFs are computed at the reported lag times
Single-component tracer displacements are extracted from trajectory data
Displacements are normalized consistently before PDF comparison
PDFs are computed for t = 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0, and 9.0 or the closest available lag times
Each empirical PDF is compared against a Gaussian distribution with the same mean and variance
Gaussianity is assessed using a two-sided Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
A two-sided KS test is implemented for empirical displacement samples against a matched Gaussian distribution
The intermediate-time t ≈ 2.0 distribution is tested for consistency with Gaussianity
The t ≈ 2.0 KS p-value is reported and compared with the target p ≈ 0.53
Excess kurtosis is computed to assess late-time platykurtic behavior
Excess kurtosis is computed for each reported lag-time displacement distribution
Late-time distributions at t ≈ 5.0 and t ≈ 9.0 are identified as light-tailed/platykurtic rather than heavy-tailed
The late-time excess kurtosis is compared with the target of approaching approximately -1.2
The analysis links negative excess kurtosis at late time to geometric saturation in the finite periodic domain
The Hill estimator is implemented to test for Lévy-flight heavy tails
A Hill estimator or equivalent tail-index estimator is applied to the displacement distribution tails
The estimated tail exponent α_L is reported
The tail exponent is compared with the target α_L ≈ -7.1
The result analysis states that the estimated tail behavior is inconsistent with Lévy-flight heavy tails in the range 0 < α_L ≤ 2
The chaotic-dynamics and vortex-ejection analyses using FTLE are implemented
Finite-Time Lyapunov Exponent calculations are implemented for tracer trajectories
A long-time FTLE or documented finite-time trajectory-separation metric is computed over the full trajectory
FTLE values are computed for all tracers or for a documented representative ensemble
The implementation accounts for periodic-domain wrapping when estimating trajectory separation
FTLE distributions for trapped and free cohorts are compared
Trapped and Free cohorts are defined consistently with the residence-time analysis
The FTLE distribution is computed for each cohort
The mean and standard deviation of FTLE are reported for each cohort
The reported cohort means are compared with the targets approximately -0.008 ± 0.013 for Trapped and -0.007 ± 0.013 for Free
The result analysis states whether the two FTLE distributions are nearly identical
The relationship between FTLE and vortex residence is analyzed
The Pearson correlation between long-time FTLE and vortex-residence fraction is computed
The correlation is compared with the target Pearson r ≈ 0.002
FTLE at vortex-exit events is computed or approximated with a documented method
The mean FTLE at vortex exit is reported and compared with the target μ ≈ -0.010
The analysis states that long-time FTLE is a weak indicator of vortex trapping or ejection dynamics in this setup
The paper's figures, numerical summaries, and scientific conclusions are reproduced
Figure 1 is reproduced
A two-dimensional slice of the Q-criterion field at z = 0 from the final simulation snapshot is plotted
Positive-Q vortex-core regions and negative-Q strain-dominated regions are visually distinguishable
Figure 2 is reproduced
The ensemble-averaged MSD curve is plotted against lag time
The Trapped and Free cohort MSD curves are plotted on the same panel or otherwise directly compared
The local scaling exponent α(t) is plotted
The reproduced figure identifies the ballistic, superdiffusive, diffusive, and saturation regimes
Figure 3 is reproduced
The dynamic anisotropy ratio λ(t) = MSD_parallel / MSD_perpendicular is plotted
The plot shows λ > 1 during the early ballistic phase and λ < 1 after approximately t = 0.5
The post-ballistic mean λ ≈ 0.52 is reported or indicated
Figure 4 is reproduced
The normalized Lagrangian autocorrelation of the Q-criterion along tracer trajectories is plotted
The 1/e threshold and τ_Q crossing are marked or reported
The reproduced figure supports τ_Q ≈ 0.200 and τ_Q/T_e ≈ 0.077
Figure 5 is reproduced
Normalized displacement PDFs are plotted at multiple lag times
A matched Gaussian reference curve is plotted for comparison
The figure shows mild early non-Gaussianity, near-Gaussian intermediate behavior, and late-time platykurtic behavior
Figures 6 and 7 are reproduced
FTLE distributions for Trapped and Free cohorts are plotted
A scatter or equivalent plot shows long-time FTLE against vortex-residence fraction
The distribution of FTLE at vortex-exit events is plotted or summarized
The reproduced outputs support the conclusion that long-time FTLE weakly distinguishes trapping dynamics
The final report contains the paper's core scientific conclusions
The report states whether MSD evolves from ballistic to superdiffusive crossover to diffusive behavior before finite-domain saturation
The report states whether transverse-dominant anisotropy is reproduced under the paper's λ convention
The report states whether vortex residence times are short relative to the large-eddy turnover time
The report states whether displacement distributions fail to develop Lévy-flight heavy tails
The report states whether late-time subdiffusive-looking behavior and light tails are attributed to finite periodic-domain saturation
The report documents any deviations from the paper's reported numerical values and distinguishes implementation uncertainty from genuine non-reproduction
